subject: business
title: The BCG Growth-Share Matrix: stars, cash cows, question marks and pets
dek: In 1970 Bruce Henderson, the founder of the Boston Consulting Group, published a two-page essay arguing that a company should be managed as a portfolio of businesses with different cash needs. Some units throw off cash, some swallow it, and the job of the head office is to move money from the first group to the most promising members of the second. The four-box picture that came out of this idea, with its stars, cash cows, question marks and pets (later 'dogs'), became one of the most widely used tools in corporate strategy. This lesson explains the framework first, then follows how General Electric, Procter & Gamble and Google used portfolio thinking, and ends with the evidence that the matrix can also lead managers astray.
era: 1960s experience-curve work, 1970 essay; cases from 1981 to 2014
honesty: The four rules, the quadrant names and the quotations from Henderson come from his essay 'The Product Portfolio' (BCG Perspectives, 1970), which BCG republishes on its website. The statement that Alan Zakon first sketched the matrix comes from the Wikipedia article on the matrix, which cites BCG's own history. The estimate that about half of Fortune 500 companies used the matrix or approaches based on it comes from BCG's 2014 'Classics Revisited' article, which cites Philippe Haspeslagh's 1982 Harvard Business Review article; it is an estimate, not a census. The GE, P&G and Google cases are examples of portfolio management in the spirit of the matrix. Welch's 'No. 1 or No. 2' rule and P&G's 2014 brand cull were not formal BCG-matrix exercises, and the Google description is BCG's own interpretation. The experimental figures are from Armstrong and Brodie's 1994 paper.

sections.title: Conglomerates, cash and the experience curve

blocks.text: In the 1950s and 1960s, many large American companies became conglomerates. A single corporation might own businesses in appliances, jet engines, chemicals, insurance and food. Each division usually kept the cash it earned and asked the head office for more when it wanted to expand. Division managers naturally argued that their own business deserved investment, and the head office, which knew far less about each market than the people running it, had no common yardstick for saying no. The result, as later writers at BCG put it, was that mature divisions often kept reinvesting their own cash at steadily falling returns, while promising new businesses were starved.

Bruce Henderson, a former Westinghouse vice president who had worked at Arthur D. Little, founded what became the Boston Consulting Group in 1963. He decided early that the firm would specialise in 'business strategy', a phrase that at the time had no settled meaning. BCG's first big idea was the experience curve. Building on the learning curve that Theodore Paul Wright had measured in aircraft factories in 1936, BCG studied cost data across many industries and found that each time a product's cumulative volume doubled, its total unit cost tended to fall by a roughly constant percentage, often somewhere between 10 and 25 per cent. From 1968 Henderson stressed the strategic meaning of this finding: the company that has produced the most will usually have the lowest costs, and the easiest way to produce the most is to hold the largest market share.

If market share drives cost, and cost drives margins and cash, then a company with many businesses can ask a simple question about each one: does it have a leading share, and is its market still growing fast enough that share can be won cheaply? Henderson's 1970 essay turned that question into a picture.

Henderson opened 'The Product Portfolio' with the claim that a successful company should own products with different growth rates and different market shares, because the mix of products determines the balance of cash flowing in and out. He then gave four rules that determine a product's cash flow.

items: Margins and cash generated are a function of market share. High share and high margins go together, which Henderson explained with the experience curve.
Growth requires cash to finance added assets. The faster a market grows, the more cash a business must spend just to hold its share.
High market share must be earned or bought, and buying share requires extra investment.
No market can grow forever. The payoff from growth must come when growth slows, in the form of cash that can no longer be usefully reinvested in that product.

blocks.text: From these rules came the matrix. The vertical axis shows the growth rate of the market. The horizontal axis shows relative market share, usually measured as the business's share divided by the share of its largest competitor, and drawn on a logarithmic scale. A ratio of 2.0 means the business is twice as large as its biggest rival; a ratio of 0.33 means the rival is three times larger. Each business is drawn as a circle whose size reflects its sales.

items: Stars: high share in a high-growth market. They usually report profits but may need all of their own cash to keep up with growth. If they keep their lead, they become cash cows when the market matures.

Cash cows: high share in a slow-growth market. They generate far more cash than they need to hold their position. Henderson argued that this surplus should not be reinvested in the same product but moved elsewhere.

Question marks (sometimes called problem children): low share in a high-growth market. They need large amounts of cash just to keep up. Unless they can be turned into leaders, they become pets when growth stops.

Pets, later usually called dogs: low share in a slow-growth market. Henderson was blunt: they may show an accounting profit, but they produce no spare cash and are 'essentially worthless, except in liquidation.'

blocks.text: The prescription follows directly. Milk the cash cows, use their cash to back the stars and a carefully chosen few question marks, and sell or close the pets. Henderson summed up the ideal: 'The balanced portfolio has stars whose high share and high growth assure the future; cash cows that supply funds for that future growth; and question marks to be converted into stars with the added funds.' Pets, he wrote, 'are not necessary. They are evidence of failure either to obtain a leadership position during the growth phase, or to get out and cut the losses.'

The matrix also implies a life cycle. A successful product usually starts as a question mark, becomes a star if the company invests to win the lead, and becomes a cash cow as its market matures. A product that never wins the lead slides from question mark to pet. The most important decisions, in Henderson's view, are therefore made early, while the market is still growing and share can be bought.

sections.title: How GE, Procter & Gamble and Google managed portfolios

blocks.text: General Electric was the classic home of portfolio planning. In the early 1970s, according to McKinsey's account, GE and McKinsey developed the nine-box matrix as a response to the same problem Henderson described. Instead of using only market growth and relative share, the nine-box grid scores each business on the attractiveness of its industry (size, growth, profitability, competition and other factors) and on the unit's competitive strength (share, costs, brand and capabilities). Units above the diagonal are candidates for investment and growth, units on the diagonal for selective investment, and units below it for harvesting, sale or closure. McKinsey notes that the framework, or a descendant of it, still underlies most large companies' formal approaches to managing business units.

In 1981, the new GE chief executive Jack Welch turned portfolio logic into a short public rule. In a speech to Wall Street analysts at the Pierre Hotel in New York, titled 'Growing Fast in a Slow-Growth Economy', he said GE would keep only businesses that were, or could become, No. 1 or No. 2 in their markets. The rest would be fixed, sold or closed. Fortune later described the speech as marking the dawn of the shareholder-value movement. Welch's rule is not the BCG matrix, but it rests on the same belief that leading share is what makes a business worth owning, and it gave managers a simple test that anyone in the company could understand.

Procter & Gamble shows the same thinking applied to brands rather than divisions. On 1 August 2014, chief executive A. G. Lafley announced that P&G would sell, discontinue or otherwise get rid of up to 100 brands over the next two years. The company would keep about 70 to 80 brands that, according to the New York Times and Bloomberg reports, generated about 90 per cent of sales and more than 95 per cent of profit. The cull followed in large deals. In November 2014 P&G agreed to transfer Duracell to Berkshire Hathaway in exchange for Berkshire's P&G shares, and in July 2015 it agreed to merge 43 beauty brands into Coty in a deal valued at the time at 12.5 billion US dollars. In matrix terms, P&G decided that many small brands were pets or weak question marks that were using managers' attention and cash without much chance of leading their categories.

Google is BCG's own modern example. In its 2014 article revisiting the matrix, BCG argued that Google kept a deliberately balanced portfolio: mature cash generators such as AdWords and AdSense, fast-growing products such as Android, and many early bets such as Glass and the driverless car. What BCG emphasised was the speed of the cycle. Google launched products such as Gmail and Glass to small groups of enthusiasts first, used data to decide which question marks to scale up, and launched and closed roughly 10 to 15 projects a year. In BCG's reading, the matrix had become a tool for running many cheap experiments and quickly killing the failures, rather than for making a few large bets.

people.name: Kevin Coyne

people.name: A. G. Lafley

people.name: Martin Reeves

blocks.text: The matrix spread quickly. BCG's 2014 article says that at its height, in the late 1970s and early 1980s, the matrix or approaches based on it were used by about half of all Fortune 500 companies, an estimate drawn from Philippe Haspeslagh's January 1982 Harvard Business Review article. Haspeslagh himself was careful about its value. He found that the grids helped head offices see what each business contributed and make clearer resource trade-offs, but the benefit came from building portfolio thinking into planning, budgeting and the way different units were managed, not from drawing the chart once.

Several criticisms followed. Market share and market growth are only two of the many things that decide whether a business is attractive, and both depend on how the market is defined: a small brand may look like a dog in 'soft drinks' and a star in 'sparkling tea'. Labelling a unit a dog can also become self-fulfilling, because managers stop investing in it and good people leave. The matrix assumes that cash can move freely inside the company and ignores links between businesses, such as a weak unit that supplies parts to a strong one. And it says little about how to turn a question mark into a star, which is where most of the real strategic work lies.

The most striking evidence came from an experiment. J. Scott Armstrong and Roderick Brodie asked 1,015 people, working individually as managers in 27 sessions in six countries over five years, to choose between two investments, one of which would clearly double the money and one of which would lose half of it. Information about the BCG matrix made people more likely to choose the unprofitable one. Of the subjects shown the matrix, 64 per cent picked the losing investment, and of those who actually used the matrix in their analysis, 87 per cent did. The matrix had taught them to prefer a 'star' over a plain calculation of returns.

BCG's own 2014 review accepted part of this criticism. Studying US public companies, it found that in 75 per cent of industries businesses moved between quadrants faster in 2008 to 2012 than in 1988 to 1992, with the average time in a quadrant falling from about four years to under two. It also found that cash cows captured a 25 per cent smaller share of total profits in 2012 than in 1982. Its conclusion was that market share is no longer a reliable predictor of performance, so the matrix should be used more often and more experimentally, with more question marks tested cheaply and pets kept 'on a short leash'.

sections.title: How the idea is used now

blocks.text: Very few companies now run their business strictly by the four boxes, but the underlying idea, that a multi-business company must deliberately move cash from mature businesses to growing ones, is still central to corporate strategy. Dow Chemical's 2012 annual report, quoted by BCG, described 'rigorously testing our portfolio to identify which businesses to grow, run for cash, fix or sell', which is almost exactly Henderson's language. The same logic is used for product ranges, brand portfolios, R&D projects and even venture capital funds, where a few winners must pay for many failures.

The matrix works best as a starting conversation rather than a verdict. It forces a company to ask which of its activities pay the bills, which ones need money now, and which ones it is keeping only out of habit. It works worst when the labels replace judgement, as the Armstrong and Brodie experiment showed.

Draw a simple growth-share matrix for cool dairy. Instead of business units, use product categories, for example vintage tees, denim, bags, accessories or band merchandise. For each one, estimate how fast demand is growing among your buyers and how strong your position is compared with the biggest sellers of that category on Carousell. Which category is your cash cow, the one that sells steadily and pays for everything else? Which is a question mark worth testing with a few listings? Which is a pet that takes sourcing time and storage space but rarely sells? Then ask the Armstrong and Brodie question: before you invest more in a 'star', have you simply checked whether it actually makes money after sourcing, cleaning, photos and shipping, given that part of the profit is meant for Taiwan women's organizations?

fun_fact.title: It was pets before it was dogs, and BCG started with 500 dollars
fun_fact.text: In Henderson's original 1970 essay the low-share, low-growth box is called 'pets', not 'dogs'; 'dogs' became the common name later. The firm that made the matrix famous began small: in its first month in 1963, the consulting division Henderson set up inside a Boston bank billed only 500 US dollars.
